Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Microfluidic systems are increasingly utilized in preclinical research, however, developing platforms that are compatible with large-scale manufacturing remains a critical challenge. In this regard, we show that thermoplastic elastomer (TPE)-based microfluidic chips could be a viable alternative to traditional poly(dimethylsiloxane) (PDMS) devices for drug testing applications. Microfluidic concentration gradient generators are essential components in these systems, enabling local spatial and temporal control of biochemical stimuli for applications such as cellular response studies and drug screening. TPEs offer key advantages, especially, optical transparency, flexibility, and compatibility with high-throughput fabrication processes compared to PDMS, thereby enhancing commercialization potential. This study demonstrates the design and fabrication of TPE-based microfluidic devices incorporating concentration gradient generators that allow precise control over solute distributions. Gradient formation was validated through numerical modeling and co-flow experiments using fluorescent dyes. The platform supported the co-culture of human lung fibroblast cells and human colon adenocarcinoma cells (HT-29), which exhibited coordinated responses to gradients of fetal bovine serum (FBS) and sepantronimum bromide (YM-155). Performance benchmarks against PDMS chips demonstrated comparable functionality, underscoring the potential of TPE-based devices for future scalable and cost-effective drug testing and cellular assays.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Inter-patient and intra-tumour heterogeneity (ITH) have prompted the need for a more personalised approach to cancer therapy. Although patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models can generate drug response specific to patients, they are not sustainable in terms of cost and time and have limited scalability. Tumour Organ-on-Chip (OoC) models are in vitro alternatives that can recapitulate some aspects of the 3D tumour microenvironment and can be scaled up for drug screening. While many tumour OoC systems have been developed to date, there have been limited validation studies to ascertain whether drug responses obtained from tumour OoCs are comparable to those predicted from patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models. In this study, we established a multiplexed tumour OoC device, that consists of an 8 × 4 array (32-plex) of culture chamber coupled to a concentration gradient generator. The device enabled perfusion culture of primary PDX-derived tumour spheroids to obtain dose-dependent response of 5 distinct standard-of-care (SOC) chemotherapeutic drugs for 3 colorectal cancer (CRC) patients. The in vitro efficacies of the chemotherapeutic drugs were rank-ordered for individual patients and compared to the in vivo efficacy obtained from matched PDX models. We show that quantitative correlation analysis between the drug efficacies predicted via the microfluidic perfusion culture is predictive of response in animal PDX models. This is a first study showing a comparative framework to quantitatively correlate the drug response predictions made by a microfluidic tumour organ-on-chip (OoC) model with that of PDX animal models.

This process has been limited in part by a lack of human-relevant preclinical models compatible with therapeutic screening on the native virus, which requires a high-containment environment. Here, we report SARS-CoV-2 infection and robust viral replication in PREDICT96-ALI, a high-throughput, human primary cell-based organ-on-chip platform. We evaluate unique infection kinetic profiles across lung tissue from three human donors by immunofluorescence, RT-qPCR, and plaque assays over a 6-day infection period. Enabled by the 96 devices/plate throughput of PREDICT96-ALI, we also investigate the efficacy of Remdesivir and MPro61 in a proof-of-concept antiviral study. Both compounds exhibit an antiviral effect against SARS-CoV-2 in the platform. This demonstration of SARS-CoV-2 infection and antiviral dosing in a high-throughput organ-on-chip platform presents a critical capability for disease modeling and therapeutic screening applications in a human physiology-relevant in vitro system.

Abstract:
Drug development suffers from a lack of predictive and human-relevant in vitro models. Organ-on-chip (OOC) technology provides advanced culture capabilities to generate physiologically appropriate, human-based tissue in vitro, therefore providing a route to a predictive in vitro model. However, OOC technologies are often created at the expense of throughput, industry-standard form factors, and compatibility with state-of-the-art data collection tools. Here we present an OOC platform with advanced culture capabilities supporting a variety of human tissue models including liver, vascular, gastrointestinal, and kidney. The platform has 96 devices per industry standard plate and compatibility with contemporary high-throughput data collection tools. Specifically, we demonstrate programmable flow control over two physiologically relevant flow regimes: perfusion flow that enhances hepatic tissue function and high-shear stress flow that aligns endothelial monolayers. In addition, we integrate electrical sensors, demonstrating quantification of barrier function of primary gut colon tissue in real-time. We utilize optical access to the tissues to directly quantify renal active transport and oxygen consumption via integrated oxygen sensors. Finally, we leverage the compatibility and throughput of the platform to screen all 96 devices using high content screening (HCS) and evaluate gene expression using RNA sequencing (RNA-seq). By combining these capabilities in one platform, physiologically-relevant tissues can be generated and measured, accelerating optimization of an in vitro model, and ultimately increasing predictive accuracy of in vitro drug screening.

Abstract:
Background In vivo-mimicking conditions are critical in in vitro cell analysis to obtain clinically relevant results. The required conditions, comparable to those prevalent in nature, can be provided by microfluidic dynamic cell cultures. Microfluidics can be used to fabricate and test the functionality and biocompatibility of newly developed nanosystems or to apply micro- and nanoelectromechanical systems embedded in a microfluidic system. However, the use of microfluidic systems is often hampered by their accessibility, acquisition cost, or customization, especially for scientists whose primary research focus is not microfluidics. Results Here we present a method for 3D printing that can be applied without special prior knowledge and sophisticated equipment to produce various ready-to-use microfluidic components with a size of 100 µm. Compared to other available methods, 3D printing using fused deposition modeling (FDM) offers several advantages, such as time-reduction and avoidance of sophisticated equipment (e.g., photolithography), as well as excellent biocompatibility and avoidance of toxic, leaching chemicals or post-processing (e.g., stereolithography). We further demonstrate the ease of use of the method for two relevant applications: a cytotoxicity screening system and an osteoblastic differentiation assay. To our knowledge, this is the first time an application including treatment, long-term cell culture and analysis on one chip has been demonstrated in a directly 3D-printed microfluidic chip. Conclusion The direct 3D printing method is tested and validated for various microfluidic components that can be combined on a chip depending on the specific requirements of the experiment. The ease of use and production opens up the potential of microfluidics to a wide range of users, especially in biomedical research. Our demonstration of its use as a cytotoxicity screening system and as an assay for osteoblastic differentiation shows the methods potential in the development of novel biomedical applications. With the presented method, we aim to disseminate microfluidics as a standard method in biomedical research, thus improving the reproducibility and transferability of results to clinical applications. Abstract:
The human microbiome significantly influences drug metabolism through the gut–liver axis, leading to modified drug responses and potential toxicity. Due to the complex nature of the human gut environment, the understanding of microbiome‐driven impacts on these processes is limited. To address this, a multiorgan‐on‐a‐chip (MOoC) platform that combines the human microbial‐crosstalk (HuMiX) gut‐on‐chip (GoC) and the Dynamic42 liver‐on‐chip (LoC), mimicking the bidirectional interconnection between the gut and liver known as the gut–liver axis, is introduced. This platform supports the viability and functionality of intestinal and liver cells. In a proof‐of‐concept study, the metabolism of irinotecan, a widely used colorectal cancer drug, is imitated within the MOoC. Utilizing liquid chromatography coupled to tandem mass spectrometry (LC‐MS/MS), irinotecan metabolites are tracked, confirming the platform's ability to represent drug metabolism along the gut–liver axis. Further, using the authors’ gut–liver platform, it is shown that the colorectal cancer‐associated gut bacterium, Escherichia coli, modifies irinotecan metabolism through the transformation of its inactive metabolite SN‐38G into its toxic metabolite SN‐38. This platform serves as a robust tool for investigating the intricate interplay between gut microbes and pharmaceuticals, offering a representative alternative to animal models and providing novel drug development strategies.

Abstract:
Measurement of cell metabolism in moderate-throughput to high-throughput organ-on-chip (OOC) systems would expand the range of data collected for studying drug effects or disease in physiologically relevant tissue models. However, current measurement approaches rely on fluorescent imaging or colorimetric assays that are focused on endpoints, require labels or added substrates, and lack real-time data. Here, we integrated optical-based oxygen sensors in a high-throughput OOC platform and developed an approach for monitoring cell metabolic activity in an array of membrane bilayer devices. Each membrane bilayer device supported a culture of human renal proximal tubule epithelial cells on a porous membrane suspended between two microchannels and exposed to controlled, unidirectional perfusion and physiologically relevant shear stress for several days. For the first time, we measured changes in oxygen in a membrane bilayer format and used a finite element analysis model to estimate cell oxygen consumption rates (OCRs), allowing comparison with OCRs from other cell culture systems. Finally, we demonstrated label-free detection of metabolic shifts in human renal proximal tubule cells following exposure to FCCP, a drug known for increasing cell oxygen consumption, as well as oligomycin and antimycin A, drugs known for decreasing cell oxygen consumption. The capability to measure cell OCRs and detect metabolic shifts in an array of membrane bilayer devices contained within an industry standard microtiter plate format will be valuable for analyzing flow-responsive and physiologically complex tissues during drug development and disease research.

Abstract:
The integration of sensing devices into cell culture systems is a topic of great interest in the study of pathologies and complex biological mechanisms in real-time. In particular, the fit-for-purpose microfluidic devices called organ-on-chip (OoC), which host living engineered organs that mimic in vivo conditions, benefit greatly from the integration of sensors, enabling the monitoring of specific chemical-physical parameters that can be correlated with biological processes. In this context, copper is an essential trace element whose total concentration may be associated with specific pathologies, and it is therefore important to develop reliable analytical techniques in cell systems. Copper can be determined by using the anodic stripping voltammetry (ASV) technique, but its applicability in cell culture media presents several challenges. Therefore, in this work, the performance of ASV in cell culture media was evaluated, and an acidification protocol was tested to improve the voltammetric signal intensity. A Transwell® culture model with Caco-2 cells was used to test the applicability of the developed acidification protocol by performing an off-line measurement. Finally, a microfluidic device was designed in order to perform the acidification of the cell culture medium in an automated manner and then integrated with a silicon microelectrode to perform in situ measurements. The resulting sensor-integrated microfluidic chip could be used to monitor the concentration of copper or other ions concentration in an organ-on-chip model; these functionalities represent a great opportunity for the non-destructive strategic experiments required on biological systems under conditions close to those in vivo.

Although promising for cancer immunotherapy, TCBs are associated with an on-target, off-tumor risk due to low levels of expression of tumor antigens in healthy tissues. The excerpt states that Tox21 compounds were prepared as DMSO stock solutions by dissolving them in anhydrous DMSO (at least 99.9% purity) to a target concentration of 20 mM. The full library was initially made in ten copies of 384-well polypropylene plates: nine copies were designated for high-throughput screening (HTS), and one for analytical quality control. The excerpt does not specify the mass weighed for each compound, the exact procedure or volume used to add DMSO, or whether compounds were weighed individually to achieve the target concentration. It also does not describe the acoustic-dispensing transfer protocol. It only indicates that HTS plates were subsequently diluted to multiple concentrations in 1536-well screening plates. A small number of compounds were prepared at 5–10 mM because of DMSO insolubility, and a few highly potent estrogenic compounds were plated at 0.2 mM. The stock plates were stored at −80 °C when not being screened or analyzed. Therefore, based on this excerpt, 20 mM is the standard stock concentration—not 10 mM—with limited exceptions.

It does, however, describe how compounds are introduced and diluted within microfluidic screening systems. Concentration gradients are produced by selecting the initial sample concentration, controlling flow rates, and designing the microchannel network. In one BACE1 assay, the compound was injected through one inlet and diluted by Taylor dispersion, while substrate and enzyme entered through separate inlets; this generated a six-order-of-magnitude concentration gradient for IC50 measurement. In another platform, a PDMS concentration-gradient generator used diffusion-based mixing, producing dose-response measurements at 23 concentrations spanning five orders of magnitude in under 30 minutes. The excerpt also notes that microfluidic systems reduce reagent consumption: an enzyme inhibition assay used 40 nL in the microdevice versus 45 µL in a 96-well plate, and an in situ click-chemistry platform used 400 nL total reaction volume. Thus, the passage supports flow- and diffusion-based on-chip dilution, but provides no evidence about weighing solids versus using pre-made DMSO stocks.

Abstract
Fragment-based screening has evolved as a remarkable approach within the drug discovery process both in the industry
and academia. Fragment screening has become a more structure-based approach to inhibitor development, but also towards
development of pathway-specific clinical probes. However, it is often witnessed that the availability, immediate and long-
term, of a high quality fragment-screening library is still beyond the reach of most academic laboratories. Within iNEXT
(Infrastructure for NMR, EM and X-rays for Translational research), a EU-funded Horizon 2020 program, a collection of
782 fragments were assembled utilizing the concept of “poised fragments” with the aim to facilitate downstream synthesis
of ligands with high affinity by fragment ligation. Herein, we describe the analytical procedure to assess the quality of this
purchased and assembled fragment library by NMR spectroscopy. This quality assessment requires buffer solubility screening,
comparison with LC/MS quality control and is supported by state-of-the-art software for high throughput data acquisition
and on-the-fly data analysis. Results from the analysis of the library are presented as a prototype of fragment progression
through the quality control process.

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Parameter | Typical values and details | Key references |
|---|---|---|
| Target master-stock concentration | **10 mM in 100% DMSO** is common in pharmaceutical collections and Echo workflows. **20 mM** is standard in Tox21, with poorly soluble compounds prepared at **5–10 mM** and exceptionally potent compounds at lower concentrations. | (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029) |
| Typical mass weighed | Published examples use approximately **2–5 mg** per compound. **1–5 mg** is therefore a practical discovery-scale range, while **10 mg or more** supplies larger-volume or repeat-use stocks. Exact mass depends on molecular weight and desired stock volume; the literature rarely reports a universal mass specification. | (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002) |
| Vessels and tracking | Solids are retained in labeled vials or automated powder stores. Solutions commonly move through **2D-barcoded tubes and racks**, polypropylene **384-well mother or source plates**, acoustic-compatible **384-well low-dead-volume plates**, and **1536-well screening or assay-ready plates**. NCATS reports automated storage for **289,000 powder vials** and **1.5 million solution tubes**. | (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000035) |
| Solvent | **Anhydrous or dry DMSO** is the default because it dissolves chemically diverse compounds and supports automated liquid handling; Tox21 specifies DMSO of at least **99.9% purity**. Water or buffer may be used for compounds unstable or insoluble in DMSO. | (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000035) |
| Solvent-addition method | Compound mass and molecular weight determine the DMSO volume required for nominal molarity. Published compound-management descriptions generally report **volumetric DMSO addition**, not gravimetric solvent addition, and often omit balance tolerance, delivered-volume uncertainty, and density correction. Concentrations may therefore remain nominal unless analytically verified. | (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029) |
| Downstream nanoliter dispensing | Echo workflows commonly load **10 mM DMSO stocks** into acoustic source plates and eject **2.5 nL droplets** or multiples thereof. One workflow loaded 30 µL of 10 mM stock per 384-well source well and transferred **5–120 nL**; another transferred **10–40 nL**, nominally 20 nL, into 1536-well assay-ready plates. | (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000032) |
| Maximum DMSO in cell assays | Cell-based assays commonly constrain final DMSO to approximately **0.1–0.5% v/v**. Representative workflows used **0.1%** in 25 µL 384-well assays and approximately **0.38%** in 4 µL 1536-well assays. DMSO backfill can equalize vehicle exposure across dose series. | (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000018) |
| Storage conditions | Working source plates may be heat-sealed under nitrogen at room temperature; longer-term copies are commonly stored under nitrogen at **−20 °C**, while Tox21 master plates are stored at **−80 °C**. Because DMSO is hygroscopic and freezes near room temperature, air exposure and freeze–thaw cycling should be minimized. | (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000035) |
| Quality control | Compound-management QC includes identity, purity, and sometimes concentration assessment by **LC–MS, GC–MS, and NMR**. Degradation, insolubility, and volatility can cause false-positive or false-negative screening results; acoustic-ejection MS can accelerate plate-level QC. | (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034) |


*Table: Typical parameters for converting discovery compounds from weighed solids into DMSO master stocks and downstream acoustic-dispensing plates. The table distinguishes concrete published values from practices that are often underreported.*

### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Platform/System | Mechanism | Dispensing Range | Accuracy/Precision | Key Bottlenecks | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mettler Toledo Quantos | Interchangeable dosing head with spiral metal impellers, rotary tapping, and gravimetric feedback | Approximately **1 mg to gram scale**, depending on powder and dosing head | At a 200 mg target for non-challenging solids: **−0.41% mean error and 1.80% SD** | Abrasive powders, coarse granules, hygroscopic or deliquescent materials, blockage, and dosing-head closure failures | About **31 s per 200 mg dose** in one comparison; **26.9% aggregate failure rate** across 13 diverse test solids (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010) |
| Chemspeed GDU-Pfd, GDU-S SWILE, and FLEX | GDU-Pfd uses a crescent-shaped valve; SWILE uses a piston, capillary, and internal balance; FLEX integrates automated powder dosing | **Sub-milligram to gram scale**, depending on module and calibration | Material-dependent; two sugar doses produced **67.0% and 85.5% errors**, although 28 other doses were near **0.2% error** | Static charge, heterogeneous particles, poor flow, hygroscopicity, blockage, cross-contamination, high cost, large footprint, maintenance, and downtime | Multiple modules broaden the usable range; **26.5% aggregate failure rate** across challenging test solids in one comparison (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010) |
| ChemBeads (AbbVie) | Reagent is coated at a known loading onto free-flowing glass beads; bead count or mass determines reagent dose | **Microgram to sub-milligram reagent quantities** | Automated 96-well dispensing typically achieved **less than 5% RSD** | Requires compound-specific bead preparation, loading calibration, characterization, storage, and compatibility validation | Reduces bridging, static buildup, and clogging by replacing neat-powder handling with standardized beads; compatible with 96- and 384-well workflows (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011) |
| Dual-arm biomimetic robot | Robot manipulates a conventional spatula above a balance using closed-loop visual and gravimetric control | Demonstrated at **20–1000 mg** targets; control tolerance reported as low as **2 mg** | At a 200 mg target for non-challenging solids: **0.07% mean error and 0.56% SD** | Slow operation, spatula clogging by compressible powders, adhesion or transformation of deliquescent materials, and occasional manipulation or balance-detection errors | Handled the widest material range; about **381 s per 200 mg sodium nitrite dose** and a **23.1% aggregate failure rate** (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010) |
| Manual weighing | Operator transfers powder with a spatula onto an analytical balance or microbalance and records the stable mass | Nominally **sub-milligram to gram scale**, subject to the balance minimum weight | Potentially accurate above the balance minimum weight; variability and transfer loss become important at low masses | Labor demand, low throughput, static, adhesion, aerosolization, hygroscopic drift, spills, exposure, transcription errors, and cross-contamination | Flexible and inexpensive for small batches but becomes a bottleneck when hundreds or thousands of individual stocks are required (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000009) |

{"answer": "## The Solid-to-Solution Step in Drug Discovery: From Weighed Powder to Liquid Stock for Nanoliter Dispensing

### 1. Overview of the Compound Management Workflow

In modern drug discovery, the conversion of solid compounds into liquid stocks is the critical upstream bottleneck that feeds all downstream nanoliter and picoliter dispensing technologies. The canonical workflow proceeds as follows: a newly synthesized compound arrives as a dry solid (typically 1–10 mg), is weighed on an analytical balance, dissolved in anhydrous DMSO to produce a concentrated master stock (usually 10 or 20 mM), transferred into 2D-barcoded tubes or polypropylene microplates, and stored frozen under inert atmosphere until needed. From these master stocks, automated liquid handlers or acoustic dispensers produce "assay-ready plates" for high-throughput screening (HTS), cell-based assays, and microfluidic/organ-on-chip drug testing (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000033).

The following table summarizes the key parameters of this solid-to-solution step as reported in the literature:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### 2. Typical Weighed Masses, Vessels, and Solvents

**Masses.** Published examples indicate that compound weighings for master stock preparation typically fall in the **1–5 mg range**, though 10 mg or more may be weighed when larger volumes of stock are required or when material is plentiful. For example, Gomez-Sanchez et al. (2020) reported using approximately 2 mg of solid to prepare a 1 mM stock in acetonitrile, while the updated workflow used pre-existing 10 mM DMSO stocks (pqac-00000002). The Tox21 program dissolved each compound at 20 mM in DMSO but did not publicly report individual per-compound masses (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029). Sou and Bergström (2018) described sub-milligram-scale dispensing into 96-well plates for automated solubility assays, where an automated solid weighing station dispensed small quantities of drug powder directly into each well (pqac-00000000).

**Vessels.** Compounds traverse several vessel types: glass or plastic vials for incoming solids, 2D-barcoded tubes in automated stores (NCATS reports capacity for 289,000 powder vials and 1.5 million solution tubes), 384-well polypropylene mother plates, acoustic-compatible 384-well low-dead-volume (LDV) plates, and 1536-well assay-ready plates (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000032).

**Solvents and target concentrations.** Anhydrous DMSO (≥99.9% purity) is the universal solvent because it dissolves structurally diverse compounds, has low volatility, and is compatible with automated liquid handling and acoustic dispensing (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000028). The standard master stock concentration is **10 mM** in pharmaceutical HTS (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013), while the Tox21 program uses **20 mM** as the default, with poorly soluble compounds prepared at 5–10 mM (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029). Water or aqueous buffer is substituted only when compounds are insoluble or unstable in DMSO (pqac-00000014).

**Solvent addition method.** Published descriptions generally indicate **volumetric** DMSO addition: a calculated volume of DMSO is pipetted into a vial or tube containing a recorded mass of solid to achieve a nominal molar concentration. True gravimetric solvent addition (weighing the DMSO to compute density-corrected volume) is not the standard practice in compound management, though it would improve accuracy. The literature rarely reports balance tolerance, delivered-volume uncertainty, or density corrections, meaning stock concentrations often remain nominal rather than analytically verified (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000028).

### 3. Downstream Nanoliter/Picoliter Dispensing Requirements

The solid-to-solution step exists to feed downstream contactless dispensing platforms, primarily:

**Acoustic droplet ejection (ADE).** The Labcyte/Beckman Echo is the dominant platform. It ejects 2.5 nL droplets from source wells containing 100% DMSO stock. Roberts et al. (2016) described an AstraZeneca workflow where 30 µL of 10 mM stock is loaded into each 384-well source well, serial dilutions are made in DMSO to produce 100 µM, 1 µM, and 10 nM source concentrations, and the Echo transfers 5–120 nL into assay wells to generate 12-point dose-response curves while maintaining final DMSO at 0.1–0.3% (pqac-00000012). Dawes et al. (2016) described a Genentech ultra-HTS system where each compound is transferred at 10–40 nL (nominally 20 nL) from sealed library source plates into 1536-well assay-ready plates (pqac-00000032). Kulesskiy et al. (2016) reported that FIMM's cancer drug sensitivity testing uses source stocks at 10 mM, 1 mM, 100 µM, and 10 µM to generate five- or nine-point dose-response curves, with Echo transfers of 2.5–25 nL into 384-well plates (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015).

**Inkjet/piezoelectric dispensers.** The Tecan D300e uses inkjet printing technology to dispense picoliter-to-nanoliter volumes directly from compound stock solutions into microplates for antimicrobial susceptibility testing and other applications (pqac-00000031).

**Microfluidic/organ-on-chip platforms.** Organ-on-chip and tumor-on-chip devices generally receive compounds from pre-made DMSO stocks (typically 1–10 mM), which are diluted into cell culture media before introduction into microfluidic channels. On-chip concentration gradient generators can produce multi-log dose-response series through diffusion-based mixing. For example, Eribol et al. (2016) described microfluidic gradient generators that produce 23 concentrations spanning five orders of magnitude in under 30 minutes, consuming only nanoliter reagent volumes (pqac-00000031). These platforms do not independently weigh solid compounds; they depend entirely on upstream stock preparation.

### 4. DMSO Stock Solution Degradation and the Need for Re-Solubilization

Several well-documented problems with DMSO stocks create a recurring need to re-dissolve compounds from the solid state:

**DMSO water uptake.** DMSO is highly hygroscopic, absorbing atmospheric moisture during every exposure (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000034). Increasing water content promotes compound precipitation and alters the solvent's properties, making stock concentrations unreliable.

**Freeze-thaw degradation.** Repeated freeze-thaw cycling reduces the fraction of compound remaining in solution, likely through precipitation of the least soluble fraction. Butler et al. (2014) reported that after storage at room temperature, 8% of compound concentrations had significantly decreased after 3 months, 17% after 6 months, and 48% after 1 year (pqac-00000035). Sou and Bergström (2018) confirmed that repeated freeze-thaw handling can reduce compound availability in concentrated stocks (pqac-00000021).

**Precipitation and solubility failures.** When DMSO stocks are diluted into aqueous assay media, poorly soluble compounds frequently precipitate, forming nanoparticles that grow and ripen over time (pqac-00000024). This produces false-negative screening results because precipitated material is unavailable to interact with the biological target. Ladisic (2023) documented that precipitated samples accumulate as incompatible with acoustic droplet ejection and must be manually removed from the chemical library (pqac-00000026). Gillespie (2013) showed that kinetic solubility measurements from DMSO stocks can overestimate thermodynamic solubility because compounds remain transiently supersaturated (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000027).

**Incomplete dissolution.** Some compounds never fully dissolve in DMSO, even at the intended stock concentration. Tox21 reported that certain compounds could only be prepared at 5–10 mM rather than the target 20 mM due to DMSO insolubility (pqac-00000028).

These degradation pathways mean that compounds must periodically be **re-solubilized from solid** to restore stock integrity, creating a recurring demand for the solid-to-solution step rather than treating it as a one-time operation.

### 5. Automated Solid Dispensing Platforms and Their Bottlenecks

The weighing step is widely recognized as the primary throughput bottleneck in compound management. Several automation solutions have been developed:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

**Mettler Toledo Quantos** uses interchangeable dosing heads with spiral metal impellers and rotary tapping. Jiang et al. (2023) reported −0.41% mean error (1.80% SD) at a 200 mg target for non-challenging solids, but a 26.9% aggregate failure rate across 13 diverse test solids due to problems with abrasive, hygroscopic, and granular materials (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000008).

**Chemspeed platforms** (GDU-Pfd, GDU-S SWILE, FLEX Powderdose) use crescent-shaped valves or piston/capillary mechanisms. They can handle sub-milligram to gram-scale dispensing but showed a 26.5% aggregate failure rate and occasional severe over-dispensing errors (67–85% for sugar) alongside near-perfect performance on other materials (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000007). Nsouli et al. (2025) noted that these systems are constrained by high cost, large physical footprint, and maintenance requirements (pqac-00000009). Tu and Wang (2026) reported that Chemspeed and Mettler Toledo systems require substantial capital investment and laboratory space, and instrument malfunctions can cause extended downtime (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000011).

**ChemBeads** (developed at AbbVie) circumvent powder-handling difficulties by coating reagents onto free-flowing glass beads at a known weight-to-weight loading ratio (typically 5% w/w). Automated dispensing of beads into 96- or 384-well plates achieved <5% RSD, effectively eliminating problems with bridging, static buildup, and clogging that plague neat-powder dispensing. However, ChemBeads require compound-specific bead preparation, loading calibration, and characterization (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000011).

**Dual-arm robotic dispensing.** Jiang et al. (2023) demonstrated a biomimetic dual-arm robot that manipulates a spatula above a balance with closed-loop gravimetric feedback. At 200 mg targets, it achieved 0.07% mean error (0.56% SD) for non-challenging solids and handled the widest material range of any tested system, but operated significantly more slowly (381 seconds vs. 31 seconds for Quantos per 200 mg dose) (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000010).

**General powder-handling bottlenecks.** Across all platforms, the fundamental challenges include electrostatic charging, hygroscopic behavior, variable bulk density, heterogeneous particle size, material adhesion to dispensing components, aerosolization, and cross-contamination between compounds (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000009). These properties are inherently compound-specific and unpredictable, which is why manual weighing—despite being slow—remains the fallback for difficult materials.

### 6. Accuracy and Precision Requirements

The accuracy required for the solid-to-solution step is moderate by analytical standards. Because downstream acoustic dispensers produce dose-response curves spanning 3–5 orders of magnitude (typically in half-log or log steps), the biological interpretation of screening data is relatively tolerant of ±10–20% errors in stock concentration. The critical requirement is that the actual concentration be **known** (or at least consistently reproducible) rather than precisely matched to a nominal target. Post-preparation analytical QC by LC-MS, GC-MS, or NMR is therefore essential for high-value compound collections (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034).

For a gravimetric powder doser targeting the 1–5 mg range, achieving ±0.1 mg (i.e., ±2–10% at 1–5 mg) would be adequate for most compound management applications, provided the actual dispensed mass is recorded and used to calculate the correct DMSO volume for the target concentration. This is precisely the "weigh solid, then add calculated solvent volume" paradigm that gravimetric dosing enables.

### 7. Relevance to an Open-Source Gravimetric Doser

An inexpensive, open-source gravimetric powder doser operating in the milligram-to-gram range would directly address the solid-to-solution bottleneck in drug discovery compound management. The target mass range (1–100+ mg) matches the quantities typically weighed for DMSO master stock preparation. The gravimetric feedback loop (load-cell balance in the dosing loop) would provide the recorded mass needed to calculate the correct DMSO volume, potentially enabling more accurate stock concentrations than the typical "weigh approximately, add nominal volume" approach. Key applications would include:

1. **Initial stock preparation** for new compound libraries (1–5 mg weighed, dissolved in DMSO to 10–20 mM)
2. **Re-solubilization** of degraded DMSO stocks from retained solid archives
3. **Solid dispensing for thermodynamic solubility assays** requiring drug powder directly in assay wells (pqac-00000000)
4. **Stock preparation for organ-on-chip/microfluidic drug screening**, where researchers typically work with commercial compounds at the bench scale and would benefit from automated weighing before manual dissolution

The open-source, low-cost design would be especially valuable for academic screening centers and microfluidic research groups that cannot justify the $100K+ investment in commercial Chemspeed or Mettler Toledo Quantos systems (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000009).

---

### Key References with Summaries

**1. Sou, T. and Bergström, C.A.S. (2018).** "Automated assays for thermodynamic (equilibrium) solubility determination." *Drug Discovery Today: Technologies*, 27, 11–19. DOI: 10.1016/j.ddtec.2018.04.004.
This review describes automated equilibrium solubility workflows that begin with 10 mM DMSO stock solutions or direct solid dispensing into 96-well plates. It recommends automated solid weighing stations for sub-milligram powder dispensing and notes that freeze-thaw handling and residual DMSO can produce unreliable solubility data (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000021).

**2. Gomez-Sanchez, R. et al. (2020).** "Method Development and Application of an Accelerated Solution Stability Screen for Drug Discovery." *SLAS Discovery*, 25, 1191–1196. DOI: 10.1177/2472555220931795.
This study reduced compound requirements for stability screening by switching from ~2 mg solid weighed into acetonitrile to pre-existing 10 mM DMSO stock solutions, illustrating the labor savings when the solid-to-solution step can be avoided (pqac-00000002).

**3. Roberts, K. et al. (2016).** "Implementation and Challenges of Direct Acoustic Dosing into Cell-Based Assays." *Journal of Laboratory Automation*, 21, 76–89. DOI: 10.1177/2211068215595212.
Details AstraZeneca's decade-long implementation of Echo acoustic dispensing. Compounds are maintained as 10 mM DMSO stocks; 30 µL is loaded per 384-well source well, serial 1:100 dilutions are made in DMSO, and the Echo transfers 2.5–120 nL into assay plates while keeping final DMSO at 0.1–0.3% (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019).

**4. Bhatt, S. et al. (2019).** "Next-Generation Compound Delivery Platforms to Support Miniaturized Biology." *SLAS Technology*, 24, 245–255. DOI: 10.1177/2472630318820017.
Describes GSK's compound delivery infrastructure including 2D-barcoded tracking, Echo 555 acoustic dispensing from 10 mM DMSO stocks, and reconstitution workflows where dispensed nanoliter volumes are evaporated and reconstituted in cell culture media (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000017).

**5. Kulesskiy, E. et al. (2016).** "Precision Cancer Medicine in the Acoustic Dispensing Era." *Journal of Laboratory Automation*, 21, 27–36. DOI: 10.1177/2211068215618869.
Describes FIMM's drug sensitivity and resistance testing platform where compounds are dissolved in DMSO at 1000× the highest assay concentration. Source plates use 10 mM, 1 mM, 100 µM, and 10 µM concentrations; Echo transfers of 2.5–25 nL generate five- or nine-point dose-response curves in 384- and 1536-well formats (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015).

**6. Dawes, T.D. et al. (2016).** "Compound Transfer by Acoustic Droplet Ejection Promotes Quality and Efficiency in Ultra-High-Throughput Screening Campaigns." *Journal of Laboratory Automation*, 21, 64–75. DOI: 10.1177/2211068215590588.
Describes Genentech's uHTS system where two Echo dispensers transfer 10–40 nL (nominally 20 nL) of DMSO-solubilized compounds from sealed library source plates into 1536-well assay-ready plates. Source plates are stored sealed at room temperature and replaced every 6 months (pqac-00000032).

**7. Jiang, Y. et al. (2023).** "Autonomous Biomimetic Solid Dispensing Using a Dual-Arm Robotic Manipulator." *Digital Discovery*, 2, 1733–1744. DOI: 10.1039/d3dd00075c.
Benchmarks a dual-arm robot against Mettler Toledo Quantos and Chemspeed across 13 diverse solids at 20–1000 mg targets. Reports mean dispensing errors of 0.07% (robot), −0.41% (Quantos), and −2.23% (Chemspeed) at 200 mg for non-challenging solids, with aggregate failure rates of 23–27% across all materials due to hygroscopic, abrasive, and compressible powder challenges (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010).

**8. Tu, N.P. and Wang, Y. (2026).** "Stick to the Beads: Supercharging Medicinal Chemistry and Methodology Development with ChemBeads." *RSC Medicinal Chemistry*, 17, 52–64. DOI: 10.1039/d5md00827a.
Reviews AbbVie's ChemBead technology, which coats reagents onto glass beads at 5% w/w loading for automated dispensing with <5% RSD. Describes compatibility with Chemspeed, Quantos, and custom robots, noting that commercial automated powder dispensers require substantial capital investment and have large footprints (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000011).

**9. Nsouli, R. et al. (2025).** "Advancing Organic Chemistry Using High-Throughput Experimentation." *Angewandte Chemie International Edition*, 64(40). DOI: 10.1002/anie.202506588.
Reviews automated solid dispensing tools for HTE, identifying Chemspeed FLEX, SWILE, Mettler Toledo CHRONECT, and XPR as recent systems capable of low-to-sub-milligram quantities. Notes that powders may be electrostatically charged, hygroscopic, or granular, creating handling errors that limit weighing reliability (pqac-00000009).

**10. Gillespie, C. (2013).** "The Precipitation of Candidate Drugs on Mixing DMSO Stock Solutions with Aqueous Buffers." *Ph.D. Dissertation*, University of Strathclyde. DOI: 10.48730/4vj6-z540.
Comprehensive study of precipitation phenomena when DMSO stocks are diluted into aqueous assay buffers. Documents that many discovery compounds precipitate upon dilution, forming nanoparticles that grow over hours. Shows that kinetic solubility from DMSO stocks overestimates thermodynamic solubility and that the physical form of precipitates (amorphous vs. crystalline) affects apparent solubility (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000027).

**11. Butler, M. et al. (2014).** "Natural Product Libraries: Assembly, Maintenance, and Screening." *Planta Medica*, 80, 1161–1170. DOI: 10.1055/s-0033-1360109.
Describes natural product compound library management including dissolution in dry DMSO and dispensing into 2D-barcoded vessels. Reports that storing DMSO stocks as frozen solids causes compound stability and solubility issues that worsen with each freeze-thaw cycle, with 48% of compounds showing significant concentration decreases after 1 year at room temperature (pqac-00000035).

**12. Sreeramulu, S. et al. (2020).** "NMR Quality Control of Fragment Libraries for Screening." *Journal of Biomolecular NMR*, 74, 555–563. DOI: 10.1007/s10858-020-00327-9.
Presents NMR-based quality control for a 782-fragment screening library. Notes that freeze-thaw cycles can result in compound degradation and that DMSO's hygroscopic nature leads to water absorption, necessitating periodic QC to ensure library integrity (pqac-00000034).

**13. Tice, R.R. et al. (2013).** "Improving the Human Hazard Characterization of Chemicals: A Tox21 Update." *Environmental Health Perspectives*, 121, 756–765. DOI: 10.1289/ehp.1205784.
Describes the Tox21 program's compound management where ~10,000 chemicals were dissolved in DMSO at a desired solubility of 20 mM and screened using 1,536-well quantitative HTS with robotic automation (pqac-00000029).

**14. Richard, A.M. et al. (2025).** "Analytical Quality Evaluation of the Tox21 Compound Library." *Chemical Research in Toxicology*, 38, 15–41. DOI: 10.1021/acs.chemrestox.4c00330.
Details the Tox21 library preparation: compounds dissolved in anhydrous DMSO (≥99.9%) at 20 mM, arrayed in ten copies of 384-well polypropylene plates, stored at −80°C. Some compounds required reduced concentrations (5–10 mM) due to DMSO insolubility. QC included LC-MS, GC-MS, and NMR (pqac-00000028).

**15. Lynch, C. et al. (2024).** "High-Throughput Screening to Advance In Vitro Toxicology: Accomplishments, Challenges, and Future Directions." *Annual Review of Pharmacology and Toxicology*, 64, 191–209. DOI: 10.1146/annurev-pharmtox-112122-104310.
Describes the NCATS compound management infrastructure including two SampleStores (capacity: 1.5 million solution tubes, 289,000 powder vials), Biomek liquid handlers for 1536-well plate preparation, and Labcyte Echo acoustic dispensers in Access workstations for assay-ready plate generation (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000033).

**16. Eribol, P. et al. (2016).** "Screening Applications in Drug Discovery Based on Microfluidic Technology." *Biomicrofluidics*, 10, 011502. DOI: 10.1063/1.4940886.
Reviews microfluidic concentration gradient generators for drug screening, demonstrating that on-chip dilution can produce dose-response measurements at 23 concentrations spanning five orders of magnitude in under 30 minutes, consuming only nanoliter reagent volumes. These platforms depend on upstream DMSO stock preparation but dramatically reduce compound consumption (pqac-00000031).

**17. Quintero, C. et al. (2013).** "High-Throughput Quality Control of DMSO Acoustic Dispensing Using Photometric Dye Methods." *SLAS Technology*, 18, 296–305. DOI: 10.1177/2211068213486787.
Validates a high-throughput photometric dual-dye QC method for monitoring Echo acoustic dispensing accuracy in the 2.5–100 nL range from 100% DMSO solutions, addressing the challenge of quality-controlling the nanoliter transfer volumes that are downstream of the solid-to-solution step."}

{"answer": "## The Solid-to-Solution Step in Drug Discovery: From Weighed Powder to Liquid Stock for Nanoliter Dispensing

### 1. Overview of the Compound Management Workflow

In modern drug discovery, the conversion of solid compounds into liquid stocks is the critical upstream bottleneck that feeds all downstream nanoliter and picoliter dispensing technologies. The canonical workflow proceeds as follows: a newly synthesized compound arrives as a dry solid (typically 1–10 mg), is weighed on an analytical balance, dissolved in anhydrous DMSO to produce a concentrated master stock (usually 10 or 20 mM), transferred into 2D-barcoded tubes or polypropylene microplates, and stored frozen under inert atmosphere until needed. From these master stocks, automated liquid handlers or acoustic dispensers produce "assay-ready plates" for high-throughput screening (HTS), cell-based assays, and microfluidic/organ-on-chip drug testing (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000033).

The following table summarizes the key parameters of this solid-to-solution step as reported in the literature:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### 2. Typical Weighed Masses, Vessels, and Solvents

**Masses.** Published examples indicate that compound weighings for master stock preparation typically fall in the **1–5 mg range**, though 10 mg or more may be weighed when larger volumes of stock are required or when material is plentiful. For example, Gomez-Sanchez et al. (2020) reported using approximately 2 mg of solid to prepare a 1 mM stock in acetonitrile, while the updated workflow used pre-existing 10 mM DMSO stocks (pqac-00000002). The Tox21 program dissolved each compound at 20 mM in DMSO but did not publicly report individual per-compound masses (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029). Sou and Bergström (2018) described sub-milligram-scale dispensing into 96-well plates for automated solubility assays, where an automated solid weighing station dispensed small quantities of drug powder directly into each well (pqac-00000000).

**Vessels.** Compounds traverse several vessel types: glass or plastic vials for incoming solids, 2D-barcoded tubes in automated stores (NCATS reports capacity for 289,000 powder vials and 1.5 million solution tubes), 384-well polypropylene mother plates, acoustic-compatible 384-well low-dead-volume (LDV) plates, and 1536-well assay-ready plates (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000032).

**Solvents and target concentrations.** Anhydrous DMSO (≥99.9% purity) is the universal solvent because it dissolves structurally diverse compounds, has low volatility, and is compatible with automated liquid handling and acoustic dispensing (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000028). The standard master stock concentration is **10 mM** in pharmaceutical HTS (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013), while the Tox21 program uses **20 mM** as the default, with poorly soluble compounds prepared at 5–10 mM (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029). Water or aqueous buffer is substituted only when compounds are insoluble or unstable in DMSO (pqac-00000014).

**Solvent addition method.** Published descriptions generally indicate **volumetric** DMSO addition: a calculated volume of DMSO is pipetted into a vial or tube containing a recorded mass of solid to achieve a nominal molar concentration. True gravimetric solvent addition (weighing the DMSO to compute density-corrected volume) is not the standard practice in compound management, though it would improve accuracy. The literature rarely reports balance tolerance, delivered-volume uncertainty, or density corrections, meaning stock concentrations often remain nominal rather than analytically verified (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000028).

### 3. Downstream Nanoliter/Picoliter Dispensing Requirements

The solid-to-solution step exists to feed downstream contactless dispensing platforms, primarily:

**Acoustic droplet ejection (ADE).** The Labcyte/Beckman Echo is the dominant platform. It ejects 2.5 nL droplets from source wells containing 100% DMSO stock. Roberts et al. (2016) described an AstraZeneca workflow where 30 µL of 10 mM stock is loaded into each 384-well source well, serial dilutions are made in DMSO to produce 100 µM, 1 µM, and 10 nM source concentrations, and the Echo transfers 5–120 nL into assay wells to generate 12-point dose-response curves while maintaining final DMSO at 0.1–0.3% (pqac-00000012). Dawes et al. (2016) described a Genentech ultra-HTS system where each compound is transferred at 10–40 nL (nominally 20 nL) from sealed library source plates into 1536-well assay-ready plates (pqac-00000032). Kulesskiy et al. (2016) reported that FIMM's cancer drug sensitivity testing uses source stocks at 10 mM, 1 mM, 100 µM, and 10 µM to generate five- or nine-point dose-response curves, with Echo transfers of 2.5–25 nL into 384-well plates (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015).

**Inkjet/piezoelectric dispensers.** The Tecan D300e uses inkjet printing technology to dispense picoliter-to-nanoliter volumes directly from compound stock solutions into microplates for antimicrobial susceptibility testing and other applications (pqac-00000031).

**Microfluidic/organ-on-chip platforms.** Organ-on-chip and tumor-on-chip devices generally receive compounds from pre-made DMSO stocks (typically 1–10 mM), which are diluted into cell culture media before introduction into microfluidic channels. On-chip concentration gradient generators can produce multi-log dose-response series through diffusion-based mixing. For example, Eribol et al. (2016) described microfluidic gradient generators that produce 23 concentrations spanning five orders of magnitude in under 30 minutes, consuming only nanoliter reagent volumes (pqac-00000031). These platforms do not independently weigh solid compounds; they depend entirely on upstream stock preparation.

### 4. DMSO Stock Solution Degradation and the Need for Re-Solubilization

Several well-documented problems with DMSO stocks create a recurring need to re-dissolve compounds from the solid state:

**DMSO water uptake.** DMSO is highly hygroscopic, absorbing atmospheric moisture during every exposure (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000034). Increasing water content promotes compound precipitation and alters the solvent's properties, making stock concentrations unreliable.

**Freeze-thaw degradation.** Repeated freeze-thaw cycling reduces the fraction of compound remaining in solution, likely through precipitation of the least soluble fraction. Butler et al. (2014) reported that after storage at room temperature, 8% of compound concentrations had significantly decreased after 3 months, 17% after 6 months, and 48% after 1 year (pqac-00000035). Sou and Bergström (2018) confirmed that repeated freeze-thaw handling can reduce compound availability in concentrated stocks (pqac-00000021).

**Precipitation and solubility failures.** When DMSO stocks are diluted into aqueous assay media, poorly soluble compounds frequently precipitate, forming nanoparticles that grow and ripen over time (pqac-00000024). This produces false-negative screening results because precipitated material is unavailable to interact with the biological target. Ladisic (2023) documented that precipitated samples accumulate as incompatible with acoustic droplet ejection and must be manually removed from the chemical library (pqac-00000026). Gillespie (2013) showed that kinetic solubility measurements from DMSO stocks can overestimate thermodynamic solubility because compounds remain transiently supersaturated (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000027).

**Incomplete dissolution.** Some compounds never fully dissolve in DMSO, even at the intended stock concentration. Tox21 reported that certain compounds could only be prepared at 5–10 mM rather than the target 20 mM due to DMSO insolubility (pqac-00000028).

These degradation pathways mean that compounds must periodically be **re-solubilized from solid** to restore stock integrity, creating a recurring demand for the solid-to-solution step rather than treating it as a one-time operation.

### 5. Automated Solid Dispensing Platforms and Their Bottlenecks

The weighing step is widely recognized as the primary throughput bottleneck in compound management. Several automation solutions have been developed:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

**Mettler Toledo Quantos** uses interchangeable dosing heads with spiral metal impellers and rotary tapping. Jiang et al. (2023) reported −0.41% mean error (1.80% SD) at a 200 mg target for non-challenging solids, but a 26.9% aggregate failure rate across 13 diverse test solids due to problems with abrasive, hygroscopic, and granular materials (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000008).

**Chemspeed platforms** (GDU-Pfd, GDU-S SWILE, FLEX Powderdose) use crescent-shaped valves or piston/capillary mechanisms. They can handle sub-milligram to gram-scale dispensing but showed a 26.5% aggregate failure rate and occasional severe over-dispensing errors (67–85% for sugar) alongside near-perfect performance on other materials (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000007). Nsouli et al. (2025) noted that these systems are constrained by high cost, large physical footprint, and maintenance requirements (pqac-00000009). Tu and Wang (2026) reported that Chemspeed and Mettler Toledo systems require substantial capital investment and laboratory space, and instrument malfunctions can cause extended downtime (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000011).

**ChemBeads** (developed at AbbVie) circumvent powder-handling difficulties by coating reagents onto free-flowing glass beads at a known weight-to-weight loading ratio (typically 5% w/w). Automated dispensing of beads into 96- or 384-well plates achieved <5% RSD, effectively eliminating problems with bridging, static buildup, and clogging that plague neat-powder dispensing. However, ChemBeads require compound-specific bead preparation, loading calibration, and characterization (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000011).

**Dual-arm robotic dispensing.** Jiang et al. (2023) demonstrated a biomimetic dual-arm robot that manipulates a spatula above a balance with closed-loop gravimetric feedback. At 200 mg targets, it achieved 0.07% mean error (0.56% SD) for non-challenging solids and handled the widest material range of any tested system, but operated significantly more slowly (381 seconds vs. 31 seconds for Quantos per 200 mg dose) (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000010).

**General powder-handling bottlenecks.** Across all platforms, the fundamental challenges include electrostatic charging, hygroscopic behavior, variable bulk density, heterogeneous particle size, material adhesion to dispensing components, aerosolization, and cross-contamination between compounds (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000009). These properties are inherently compound-specific and unpredictable, which is why manual weighing—despite being slow—remains the fallback for difficult materials.

### 6. Accuracy and Precision Requirements

The accuracy required for the solid-to-solution step is moderate by analytical standards. Because downstream acoustic dispensers produce dose-response curves spanning 3–5 orders of magnitude (typically in half-log or log steps), the biological interpretation of screening data is relatively tolerant of ±10–20% errors in stock concentration. The critical requirement is that the actual concentration be **known** (or at least consistently reproducible) rather than precisely matched to a nominal target. Post-preparation analytical QC by LC-MS, GC-MS, or NMR is therefore essential for high-value compound collections (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034).

For a gravimetric powder doser targeting the 1–5 mg range, achieving ±0.1 mg (i.e., ±2–10% at 1–5 mg) would be adequate for most compound management applications, provided the actual dispensed mass is recorded and used to calculate the correct DMSO volume for the target concentration. This is precisely the "weigh solid, then add calculated solvent volume" paradigm that gravimetric dosing enables.

### 7. Relevance to an Open-Source Gravimetric Doser

An inexpensive, open-source gravimetric powder doser operating in the milligram-to-gram range would directly address the solid-to-solution bottleneck in drug discovery compound management. The target mass range (1–100+ mg) matches the quantities typically weighed for DMSO master stock preparation. The gravimetric feedback loop (load-cell balance in the dosing loop) would provide the recorded mass needed to calculate the correct DMSO volume, potentially enabling more accurate stock concentrations than the typical "weigh approximately, add nominal volume" approach. Key applications would include:

1. **Initial stock preparation** for new compound libraries (1–5 mg weighed, dissolved in DMSO to 10–20 mM)
2. **Re-solubilization** of degraded DMSO stocks from retained solid archives
3. **Solid dispensing for thermodynamic solubility assays** requiring drug powder directly in assay wells (pqac-00000000)
4. **Stock preparation for organ-on-chip/microfluidic drug screening**, where researchers typically work with commercial compounds at the bench scale and would benefit from automated weighing before manual dissolution

The open-source, low-cost design would be especially valuable for academic screening centers and microfluidic research groups that cannot justify the $100K+ investment in commercial Chemspeed or Mettler Toledo Quantos systems (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000009).

---

### Key References with Summaries

**1. Sou, T. and Bergström, C.A.S. (2018).** "Automated assays for thermodynamic (equilibrium) solubility determination." *Drug Discovery Today: Technologies*, 27, 11–19. DOI: 10.1016/j.ddtec.2018.04.004.
This review describes automated equilibrium solubility workflows that begin with 10 mM DMSO stock solutions or direct solid dispensing into 96-well plates. It recommends automated solid weighing stations for sub-milligram powder dispensing and notes that freeze-thaw handling and residual DMSO can produce unreliable solubility data (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000021).

**2. Gomez-Sanchez, R. et al. (2020).** "Method Development and Application of an Accelerated Solution Stability Screen for Drug Discovery." *SLAS Discovery*, 25, 1191–1196. DOI: 10.1177/2472555220931795.
This study reduced compound requirements for stability screening by switching from ~2 mg solid weighed into acetonitrile to pre-existing 10 mM DMSO stock solutions, illustrating the labor savings when the solid-to-solution step can be avoided (pqac-00000002).

**3. Roberts, K. et al. (2016).** "Implementation and Challenges of Direct Acoustic Dosing into Cell-Based Assays." *Journal of Laboratory Automation*, 21, 76–89. DOI: 10.1177/2211068215595212.
Details AstraZeneca's decade-long implementation of Echo acoustic dispensing. Compounds are maintained as 10 mM DMSO stocks; 30 µL is loaded per 384-well source well, serial 1:100 dilutions are made in DMSO, and the Echo transfers 2.5–120 nL into assay plates while keeping final DMSO at 0.1–0.3% (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019).

**4. Bhatt, S. et al. (2019).** "Next-Generation Compound Delivery Platforms to Support Miniaturized Biology." *SLAS Technology*, 24, 245–255. DOI: 10.1177/2472630318820017.
Describes GSK's compound delivery infrastructure including 2D-barcoded tracking, Echo 555 acoustic dispensing from 10 mM DMSO stocks, and reconstitution workflows where dispensed nanoliter volumes are evaporated and reconstituted in cell culture media (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000017).

**5. Kulesskiy, E. et al. (2016).** "Precision Cancer Medicine in the Acoustic Dispensing Era." *Journal of Laboratory Automation*, 21, 27–36. DOI: 10.1177/2211068215618869.
Describes FIMM's drug sensitivity and resistance testing platform where compounds are dissolved in DMSO at 1000× the highest assay concentration. Source plates use 10 mM, 1 mM, 100 µM, and 10 µM concentrations; Echo transfers of 2.5–25 nL generate five- or nine-point dose-response curves in 384- and 1536-well formats (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015).

**6. Dawes, T.D. et al. (2016).** "Compound Transfer by Acoustic Droplet Ejection Promotes Quality and Efficiency in Ultra-High-Throughput Screening Campaigns." *Journal of Laboratory Automation*, 21, 64–75. DOI: 10.1177/2211068215590588.
Describes Genentech's uHTS system where two Echo dispensers transfer 10–40 nL (nominally 20 nL) of DMSO-solubilized compounds from sealed library source plates into 1536-well assay-ready plates. Source plates are stored sealed at room temperature and replaced every 6 months (pqac-00000032).

**7. Jiang, Y. et al. (2023).** "Autonomous Biomimetic Solid Dispensing Using a Dual-Arm Robotic Manipulator." *Digital Discovery*, 2, 1733–1744. DOI: 10.1039/d3dd00075c.
Benchmarks a dual-arm robot against Mettler Toledo Quantos and Chemspeed across 13 diverse solids at 20–1000 mg targets. Reports mean dispensing errors of 0.07% (robot), −0.41% (Quantos), and −2.23% (Chemspeed) at 200 mg for non-challenging solids, with aggregate failure rates of 23–27% across all materials due to hygroscopic, abrasive, and compressible powder challenges (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010).

**8. Tu, N.P. and Wang, Y. (2026).** "Stick to the Beads: Supercharging Medicinal Chemistry and Methodology Development with ChemBeads." *RSC Medicinal Chemistry*, 17, 52–64. DOI: 10.1039/d5md00827a.
Reviews AbbVie's ChemBead technology, which coats reagents onto glass beads at 5% w/w loading for automated dispensing with <5% RSD. Describes compatibility with Chemspeed, Quantos, and custom robots, noting that commercial automated powder dispensers require substantial capital investment and have large footprints (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000011).

**9. Nsouli, R. et al. (2025).** "Advancing Organic Chemistry Using High-Throughput Experimentation." *Angewandte Chemie International Edition*, 64(40). DOI: 10.1002/anie.202506588.
Reviews automated solid dispensing tools for HTE, identifying Chemspeed FLEX, SWILE, Mettler Toledo CHRONECT, and XPR as recent systems capable of low-to-sub-milligram quantities. Notes that powders may be electrostatically charged, hygroscopic, or granular, creating handling errors that limit weighing reliability (pqac-00000009).

**10. Gillespie, C. (2013).** "The Precipitation of Candidate Drugs on Mixing DMSO Stock Solutions with Aqueous Buffers." *Ph.D. Dissertation*, University of Strathclyde. DOI: 10.48730/4vj6-z540.
Comprehensive study of precipitation phenomena when DMSO stocks are diluted into aqueous assay buffers. Documents that many discovery compounds precipitate upon dilution, forming nanoparticles that grow over hours. Shows that kinetic solubility from DMSO stocks overestimates thermodynamic solubility and that the physical form of precipitates (amorphous vs. crystalline) affects apparent solubility (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000027).

**11. Butler, M. et al. (2014).** "Natural Product Libraries: Assembly, Maintenance, and Screening." *Planta Medica*, 80, 1161–1170. DOI: 10.1055/s-0033-1360109.
Describes natural product compound library management including dissolution in dry DMSO and dispensing into 2D-barcoded vessels. Reports that storing DMSO stocks as frozen solids causes compound stability and solubility issues that worsen with each freeze-thaw cycle, with 48% of compounds showing significant concentration decreases after 1 year at room temperature (pqac-00000035).

**12. Sreeramulu, S. et al. (2020).** "NMR Quality Control of Fragment Libraries for Screening." *Journal of Biomolecular NMR*, 74, 555–563. DOI: 10.1007/s10858-020-00327-9.
Presents NMR-based quality control for a 782-fragment screening library. Notes that freeze-thaw cycles can result in compound degradation and that DMSO's hygroscopic nature leads to water absorption, necessitating periodic QC to ensure library integrity (pqac-00000034).

**13. Tice, R.R. et al. (2013).** "Improving the Human Hazard Characterization of Chemicals: A Tox21 Update." *Environmental Health Perspectives*, 121, 756–765. DOI: 10.1289/ehp.1205784.
Describes the Tox21 program's compound management where ~10,000 chemicals were dissolved in DMSO at a desired solubility of 20 mM and screened using 1,536-well quantitative HTS with robotic automation (pqac-00000029).

**14. Richard, A.M. et al. (2025).** "Analytical Quality Evaluation of the Tox21 Compound Library." *Chemical Research in Toxicology*, 38, 15–41. DOI: 10.1021/acs.chemrestox.4c00330.
Details the Tox21 library preparation: compounds dissolved in anhydrous DMSO (≥99.9%) at 20 mM, arrayed in ten copies of 384-well polypropylene plates, stored at −80°C. Some compounds required reduced concentrations (5–10 mM) due to DMSO insolubility. QC included LC-MS, GC-MS, and NMR (pqac-00000028).

**15. Lynch, C. et al. (2024).** "High-Throughput Screening to Advance In Vitro Toxicology: Accomplishments, Challenges, and Future Directions." *Annual Review of Pharmacology and Toxicology*, 64, 191–209. DOI: 10.1146/annurev-pharmtox-112122-104310.
Describes the NCATS compound management infrastructure including two SampleStores (capacity: 1.5 million solution tubes, 289,000 powder vials), Biomek liquid handlers for 1536-well plate preparation, and Labcyte Echo acoustic dispensers in Access workstations for assay-ready plate generation (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000033).

**16. Eribol, P. et al. (2016).** "Screening Applications in Drug Discovery Based on Microfluidic Technology." *Biomicrofluidics*, 10, 011502. DOI: 10.1063/1.4940886.
Reviews microfluidic concentration gradient generators for drug screening, demonstrating that on-chip dilution can produce dose-response measurements at 23 concentrations spanning five orders of magnitude in under 30 minutes, consuming only nanoliter reagent volumes. These platforms depend on upstream DMSO stock preparation but dramatically reduce compound consumption (pqac-00000031).

**17. Quintero, C. et al. (2013).** "High-Throughput Quality Control of DMSO Acoustic Dispensing Using Photometric Dye Methods." *SLAS Technology*, 18, 296–305. DOI: 10.1177/2211068213486787.
Validates a high-throughput photometric dual-dye QC method for monitoring Echo acoustic dispensing accuracy in the 2.5–100 nL range from 100% DMSO solutions, addressing the challenge of quality-controlling the nanoliter transfer volumes that are downstream of the solid-to-solution step."}

In modern drug discovery, the conversion of solid compounds into liquid stocks is the critical upstream bottleneck that feeds all downstream nanoliter and picoliter dispensing technologies. The canonical workflow proceeds as follows: a newly synthesized compound arrives as a dry solid (typically 1–10 mg), is weighed on an analytical balance, dissolved in anhydrous DMSO to produce a concentrated master stock (usually 10 or 20 mM), transferred into 2D-barcoded tubes or polypropylene microplates, and stored frozen under inert atmosphere until needed. From these master stocks, automated liquid handlers or acoustic dispensers produce "assay-ready plates" for high-throughput screening (HTS), cell-based assays, and microfluidic/organ-on-chip drug testing (bhatt2019nextgenerationcompounddelivery pages 2-4, lynch2024highthroughputscreeningto pages 3-4).

### 2. Typical Weighed Masses, Vessels, and Solvents

**Masses.** Published examples indicate that compound weighings for master stock preparation typically fall in the **1–5 mg range**, though 10 mg or more may be weighed when larger volumes of stock are required or when material is plentiful. For example, Gomez-Sanchez et al. (2020) reported using approximately 2 mg of solid to prepare a 1 mM stock in acetonitrile, while the updated workflow used pre-existing 10 mM DMSO stocks (gomezsanchez2020methoddevelopmentand pages 1-2). The Tox21 program dissolved each compound at 20 mM in DMSO but did not publicly report individual per-compound masses (richard2025analyticalqualityevaluation pages 3-4, tice2013improvingthehuman pages 1-2). Sou and Bergström (2018) described sub-milligram-scale dispensing into 96-well plates for automated solubility assays, where an automated solid weighing station dispensed small quantities of drug powder directly into each well (sou2018automatedassaysfor pages 3-5).

**Vessels.** Compounds traverse several vessel types: glass or plastic vials for incoming solids, 2D-barcoded tubes in automated stores (NCATS reports capacity for 289,000 powder vials and 1.5 million solution tubes), 384-well polypropylene mother plates, acoustic-compatible 384-well low-dead-volume (LDV) plates, and 1536-well assay-ready plates (bhatt2019nextgenerationcompounddelivery pages 2-4, lynch2024highthroughputscreeningto pages 3-4, dawes2016compoundtransferby pages 2-3).

**Solvents and target concentrations.** Anhydrous DMSO (≥99.9% purity) is the universal solvent because it dissolves structurally diverse compounds, has low volatility, and is compatible with automated liquid handling and acoustic dispensing (gillespie2013theprecipitationof pages 10-15, richard2025analyticalqualityevaluation pages 3-4). The standard master stock concentration is **10 mM** in pharmaceutical HTS (roberts2016implementationandchallenges pages 2-3, bhatt2019nextgenerationcompounddelivery pages 2-4), while the Tox21 program uses **20 mM** as the default, with poorly soluble compounds prepared at 5–10 mM (richard2025analyticalqualityevaluation pages 3-4, tice2013improvingthehuman pages 1-2). Water or aqueous buffer is substituted only when compounds are insoluble or unstable in DMSO (kulesskiy2016precisioncancermedicine pages 2-3).

**Solvent addition method.** Published descriptions generally indicate **volumetric** DMSO addition: a calculated volume of DMSO is pipetted into a vial or tube containing a recorded mass of solid to achieve a nominal molar concentration. True gravimetric solvent addition (weighing the DMSO to compute density-corrected volume) is not the standard practice in compound management, though it would improve accuracy. The literature rarely reports balance tolerance, delivered-volume uncertainty, or density corrections, meaning stock concentrations often remain nominal rather than analytically verified (gomezsanchez2020methoddevelopmentand pages 1-2, richard2025analyticalqualityevaluation pages 3-4).

### 3. Downstream Nanoliter/Picoliter Dispensing Requirements

The solid-to-solution step exists to feed downstream contactless dispensing platforms, primarily:

**Acoustic droplet ejection (ADE).** The Labcyte/Beckman Echo is the dominant platform. It ejects 2.5 nL droplets from source wells containing 100% DMSO stock. Roberts et al. (2016) described an AstraZeneca workflow where 30 µL of 10 mM stock is loaded into each 384-well source well, serial dilutions are made in DMSO to produce 100 µM, 1 µM, and 10 nM source concentrations, and the Echo transfers 5–120 nL into assay wells to generate 12-point dose-response curves while maintaining final DMSO at 0.1–0.3% (roberts2016implementationandchallenges pages 2-3). Dawes et al. (2016) described a Genentech ultra-HTS system where each compound is transferred at 10–40 nL (nominally 20 nL) from sealed library source plates into 1536-well assay-ready plates (dawes2016compoundtransferby pages 2-3). Kulesskiy et al. (2016) reported that FIMM's cancer drug sensitivity testing uses source stocks at 10 mM, 1 mM, 100 µM, and 10 µM to generate five- or nine-point dose-response curves, with Echo transfers of 2.5–25 nL into 384-well plates (kulesskiy2016precisioncancermedicine pages 2-3, kulesskiy2016precisioncancermedicine pages 3-7).

**Inkjet/piezoelectric dispensers.** The Tecan D300e uses inkjet printing technology to dispense picoliter-to-nanoliter volumes directly from compound stock solutions into microplates for antimicrobial susceptibility testing and other applications (eribol2016screeningapplicationsin pages 7-9).

**Microfluidic/organ-on-chip platforms.** Organ-on-chip and tumor-on-chip devices generally receive compounds from pre-made DMSO stocks (typically 1–10 mM), which are diluted into cell culture media before introduction into microfluidic channels. On-chip concentration gradient generators can produce multi-log dose-response series through diffusion-based mixing. For example, Eribol et al. (2016) described microfluidic gradient generators that produce 23 concentrations spanning five orders of magnitude in under 30 minutes, consuming only nanoliter reagent volumes (eribol2016screeningapplicationsin pages 7-9). These platforms do not independently weigh solid compounds; they depend entirely on upstream stock preparation.

### 4. DMSO Stock Solution Degradation and the Need for Re-Solubilization

Several well-documented problems with DMSO stocks create a recurring need to re-dissolve compounds from the solid state:

**DMSO water uptake.** DMSO is highly hygroscopic, absorbing atmospheric moisture during every exposure (gillespie2013theprecipitationof pages 25-29, sreeramulu2020nmrqualitycontrol pages 1-2). Increasing water content promotes compound precipitation and alters the solvent's properties, making stock concentrations unreliable.

**Freeze-thaw degradation.** Repeated freeze-thaw cycling reduces the fraction of compound remaining in solution, likely through precipitation of the least soluble fraction. Butler et al. (2014) reported that after storage at room temperature, 8% of compound concentrations had significantly decreased after 3 months, 17% after 6 months, and 48% after 1 year (butler2014naturalproductlibraries pages 3-4). Sou and Bergström (2018) confirmed that repeated freeze-thaw handling can reduce compound availability in concentrated stocks (sou2018automatedassaysfor pages 2-3).

**Precipitation and solubility failures.** When DMSO stocks are diluted into aqueous assay media, poorly soluble compounds frequently precipitate, forming nanoparticles that grow and ripen over time (gillespie2013theprecipitationof pages 70-76). This produces false-negative screening results because precipitated material is unavailable to interact with the biological target. Ladisic (2023) documented that precipitated samples accumulate as incompatible with acoustic droplet ejection and must be manually removed from the chemical library (ladisic2023theeffectof pages 19-23). Gillespie (2013) showed that kinetic solubility measurements from DMSO stocks can overestimate thermodynamic solubility because compounds remain transiently supersaturated (gillespie2013theprecipitationof pages 32-35, gillespie2013theprecipitationof pages 29-32).

**Incomplete dissolution.** Some compounds never fully dissolve in DMSO, even at the intended stock concentration. Tox21 reported that certain compounds could only be prepared at 5–10 mM rather than the target 20 mM due to DMSO insolubility (richard2025analyticalqualityevaluation pages 3-4).

These degradation pathways mean that compounds must periodically be **re-solubilized from solid** to restore stock integrity, creating a recurring demand for the solid-to-solution step rather than treating it as a one-time operation.
