| Solvent-addition method | Compound mass and molecular weight determine the DMSO volume required for nominal molarity. Published compound-management descriptions generally report **volumetric DMSO addition**, not gravimetric solvent addition, and often omit balance tolerance, delivered-volume uncertainty, and density correction. Concentrations may therefore remain nominal unless analytically verified. | (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029) |
| Downstream nanoliter dispensing | Echo workflows commonly load **10 mM DMSO stocks** into acoustic source plates and eject **2.5 nL droplets** or multiples thereof. One workflow loaded 30 µL of 10 mM stock per 384-well source well and transferred **5–120 nL**; another transferred **10–40 nL**, nominally 20 nL, into 1536-well assay-ready plates. | (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000032) |
| Maximum DMSO in cell assays | Cell-based assays commonly constrain final DMSO to approximately **0.1–0.5% v/v**. Representative workflows used **0.1%** in 25 µL 384-well assays and approximately **0.38%** in 4 µL 1536-well assays. DMSO backfill can equalize vehicle exposure across dose series. | (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000018) |
| Storage conditions | Working source plates may be heat-sealed under nitrogen at room temperature; longer-term copies are commonly stored under nitrogen at **−20 °C**, while Tox21 master plates are stored at **−80 °C**. Because DMSO is hygroscopic and freezes near room temperature, air exposure and freeze–thaw cycling should be minimized. | (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000035) |
| Quality control | Compound-management QC includes identity, purity, and sometimes concentration assessment by **LC–MS, GC–MS, and NMR**. Degradation, insolubility, and volatility can cause false-positive or false-negative screening results; acoustic-ejection MS can accelerate plate-level QC. | (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034) |


*Table: Typical parameters for converting discovery compounds from weighed solids into DMSO master stocks and downstream acoustic-dispensing plates. The table distinguishes concrete published values from practices that are often underreported.*

info.query: Context: we are developing an inexpensive, open-source, gravimetric powder doser (auger / vibratory feed with a load-cell balance in the loop) for self-driving laboratories. It was designed for multi-powder dosing of metal powders for additive-manufacturing alloy discovery and targets the milligram-to-gram range; it is not intended for sub-milligram dosing. We want to know where it could be useful in drug discovery, in particular as the upstream 'weigh solid into a vial, then dissolve' step that precedes far smaller (nanoliter-to-picoliter) liquid dispensing onto microplates or lab-on-a-chip / organ-on-chip devices. In current automated drug discovery workflows (compound management, high-throughput screening, cell-based and phenotypic assays, and microfluidic / lab-on-a-chip / organ-on-chip / tumor-on-chip drug screening), how are solid compounds converted into the liquid stocks that downstream nanoliter/picoliter dispensers consume (acoustic droplet ejection such as the Labcyte/Beckman Echo, pin tools, piezoelectric or inkjet dispensers such as the Tecan D300e, and on-chip dilution / concentration-gradient generators)? Describe the 'solid-to-solution' step in detail: typical weighed masses (sub-mg, 1-5 mg, 10-100 mg, gram scale), vessels (vials, 2D-barcoded tubes, plates), solvents (DMSO, water, buffer), target concentrations (e.g. 10 mM DMSO master stocks), whether solvent is added volumetrically or gravimetrically to hit a target concentration from the recorded mass, and the accuracy/precision actually required. Identify the published automation solutions and their bottlenecks (manual weighing labor, electrostatic / cohesive / hygroscopic / sticky APIs, cross-contamination, incomplete dissolution and solubility failures, DMSO water uptake and freeze-thaw degradation that force re-solubilization from solid), and quantify throughput (weighings/day), labor and cost where reported. For each key source give a full citation (authors, year, journal, DOI) and a 2-4 sentence summary. Aim for 12-20 references, emphasizing 2010-2026 peer-reviewed work (e.g. SLAS Discovery, SLAS Technology / JALA, Drug Discovery Today, Lab on a Chip, Organic Process Research & Development).
